title: Gravity Guild V2: I dropped image-gen art and now all 50 characters come from a Blender Python script. Free co-op gravity game in your browser
author: keens007
selftext:
Gravity Guild is a free co-op 3D game that runs in your browser. You flip your own gravity, carry Gravity Cores across floating sky islands and deliver them to the Relay before the timer runs out. 1 to 8 players, with keyboard/mouse, gamepad or touch.

How AI fits in: the game is built in Godot 4.7, and most of the GDScript was written with Claude Code, an AI coding assistant. The bigger lesson for me was the art. The V1 key art came from an image generator. It looked AI-made, and it showed characters that weren't even in the game. For V2 I dropped image generation entirely. All 50 playable characters, the trees, props and gloves now come out of a single Blender Python script, the logo is custom lettering built from geometry (no font), and the menu backdrop is rendered in-engine. Because the models are generated from code, I can change the whole roster and rebuild it with one command, and the menu art finally matches what you see in game.

New in V2: 50 crew members (no two players in a game share one), 6 skies with their own biome and time of day, 4 modes (Relay Run, Core Rush, Time Trial, Free Build), random round modifiers like Low Gravity and Gravity Storm, first or third person, online room codes and proximity voice chat.

Play free: [https://promptkettle.itch.io/gravity-guild](https://promptkettle.itch.io/gravity-guild)

Looking for feedback: is the gravity flip readable in the trailer, or confusing? And has anyone else here moved from image-gen assets to procedural/scripted models? Curious how it went for you.

comments.author: VictorBuildsApps
comments.body:
I did this for props rather than characters. A small web game of mine had about 140 models built in code, and agents rewrote them as Python scripts that run in Blender, packed into one GLB. We kept every footprint and pivot from the old models, so nothing in the game had to move.

What bit me was the ambient occlusion bake. Rebaking from unchanged scripts still gave slightly different vertex colors, so when one piece needed a fix I rebuilt only that piece and checked that the other 139 matched the reviewed copy, instead of rebaking everything.

Characters went worse. A scripted creature head looked fine at mid distance and failed in a close-up review, so for characters I now generate the parts and assemble them in Blender. How are your 50 holding up at the camera distance of the real game, and do you rebuild the whole roster each time or only what changed?
